[860] International security and defense cooperation

[861] A solid international framework serves Norway's interests, and the government will work towards the further development of a global multilateral legal order based on the principles enshrined in the UN Charter

[862] The NATO alliance and the transatlantic security community are the pillars of Norwegian security policy

[863] Norway depends on strong and close international security and defense cooperation

[864] Our most important European partners are members of the EU, which is a key partner for Norway

[865] Today's and tomorrow's security challenges must be solved through collaboration

[866] The government is based on an active alliance policy in which NATO is linked more closely to Norway and Norwegian interests in everyday life, in crises and in armed conflict

[867] An active alliance policy aims to reduce the risk of security crises and armed conflict

[868] An attack against a NATO member is considered an attack against the entire alliance

[869] This means that serious threats to Norway must be handled within the framework of NATO's collective defense

[870] Developments in NATO are therefore crucial for Norwegian security

[871] NATO must have a deterrent effect that reduces the risk of threats and attacks against the territory of its member states

[872] Adequate preparedness and credible defense capabilities are necessary to meet the security challenges facing the alliance

[873] An active alliance policy requires a strong national defense, substantial contributions to burden-sharing and international efforts, strengthening NATO's collective defense, and close relations with important allies

[874] The mutual guarantee of NATO cooperation also means that Norway will be obliged to support other allies in the event of threats, attacks or attacks

[875] NATO is a political and military alliance

[876] The transatlantic security community based on shared values ​​forms the core

[877] Economic challenges and increasing political polarization in Europe pose a challenge to the further development of NATO

[878] The economic crisis has left its mark on the alliance, and the countries that have been hardest hit have cut their defense budgets the most

[879] The alliance will still be dependent on the United States for key capabilities, particularly in the event of major operations related to collective defense, or when the alliance is engaged in several locations simultaneously

[880] In this situation, it is therefore crucial to maintain NATO's relevance to the United States and ensure continued American engagement and presence in Europe

[881] The United States accounts for about 70 percent of the alliance's total defense spending and has long made it clear that this uneven burden sharing cannot continue

[882] While the United States maintains its commitment in Europe, developments in the Asia-Pacific region indicate that significant American military resources will be available in this region

[883] The United States expects European NATO countries to take greater responsibility for their own security, through increased contributions to burden sharing and by meeting the long-term goal from the NATO summit in Wales in September 2014 to increase defense budgets

[884] The goal from the summit is to increase defense budgets to 2 percent of GDP by 2024, and to spend 20 percent of defense budgets on investments

[885] In the short term, it is important to reverse the cuts in member states' defense budgets

[886] The rising costs of acquiring and operating military equipment make cooperation with close allies increasingly important

[887] Better burden sharing can be achieved by European allies demonstrating their willingness and ability to invest in and modernize their own defense, as well as fill NATO's capability gaps, contribute to security in their immediate areas, and make significant contributions to operations and capacity building, also outside the alliance's territory

[888] For Norway, it is also about taking responsibility and being a predictable and credible ally

[889] Many years of crisis management operations outside the alliance's territory have weakened the capacity to plan for crises and armed conflicts involving one's own territory

[890] In recent years, the Alliance has placed renewed emphasis on deterrence and collective defense capabilities

[891] Several measures to strengthen NATO's operational capability through enhanced preparedness, response capability and presence demonstrate the Alliance's ability to adapt to the new security policy situation in Europe, and signal support for and solidarity with those of the Alliance's member states that feel most vulnerable

[892] Norway has maintained its defense investments

[893] In the future, it will be important that NATO member states, including Norway, contribute in solidarity to the alliance's burden sharing

[894] Norway will continue to fill its share of NATO's force structure, including making sufficient contributions to NATO's readiness forces, including standing maritime forces and air forces

[895] Contribution to NATO

[896] Force (NRF) to maintain allied interoperability and a credible deterrent capability is particularly relevant

[897] Norway also has an important responsibility on behalf of NATO in the North to contribute to the alliance's situational awareness and to assert sovereignty

[898] The Storting unanimously met in Stipulation

[899] S (2015–2016) on Norwegian policy on nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation

[900] The Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) is the foundation for global efforts on nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament

[901] The goal is a world without nuclear weapons, based on binding and verifiable agreements that include all countries

[902] NATO's Deterrence and Defence Posture Review from 2012 includes both a conventional and a nuclear component, as well as missile defence

[903] Today's and future security challenges make it necessary to view these components in context, in order to achieve the necessary deterrence

[904] The most important function of nuclear weapons is to deter threats or use of nuclear weapons against NATO member states

[905] This is based on both the American and NATO nuclear weapons policies, which affirm that as long as there are nuclear weapons in the world, NATO will be an alliance with nuclear weapons

[906] NATO also plays an important role in disarmament and non-proliferation efforts, and has unilaterally disarmed 97 percent of its nuclear weapons since the Cold War

[907] All NATO countries are parties to the NPT, and NATO supports the NPT's goal of a world without nuclear weapons

[908] The alliance advocates increased transparency about short-range nuclear weapons in Europe, as well as a reduction in the number of such weapons in agreements with Russia

[909] This is demanding in the current security policy situation

[910] Although the security policy basis for nuclear disarmament between the United States and Russia is not present today, it is crucial to help lay the foundation for future disarmament

[911] A good example of this is Norway's involvement in the verification of nuclear disarmament, where Norway cooperates closely with the United Kingdom and the United States

[912] The goal of a global multilateral legal order based on the principles enshrined in the UN Charter underlies Norwegian foreign and security policy

[913] As a framework for international cooperation, the UN is the central, global actor that must ensure that relations between states are based on international law and respect for human rights

[914] A well-functioning set of international law rules is crucial for Norway's ability to promote and safeguard its interests

[915] The UN Security Council's ability to handle global and regional challenges is hampered by internal disagreements among the council's permanent members

[916] Russia and China base their decisions on different interpretations of international law that have great significance for international stability and the protection of civilians

[917] The shifts in global power structures may contribute to weakening the Security Council's legitimacy and, in the long term, could also weaken the Council's effectiveness

[918] UN peacekeeping operations are a key instrument for preventing, limiting and ending conflicts

[919] The operations have a focus on conflict areas in Africa and the Middle East

[920] Norway has a responsibility and a vested interest in contributing to UN peacekeeping operations

[921] Initiatives to reform and strengthen UN peacekeeping operations could make them more modern and relevant

[922] The Government has placed emphasis on being an active contributor to the UN reform process, including in connection with the UN High-Level Panel and the initiative to mobilize resources for UN peacekeeping operations

[923] It will be particularly important to improve the mobilization of personnel, resources and capabilities

[924] Until further notice, the protection of civilians and the gender perspective should be seen in the context of, and be an integral part of, military peace operations

[925] For military efforts within a UN framework, Norway preferably provides force contributions together with close allies and/or partners

[926] Norway will prioritize providing sought-after niche capacities of great importance to the UN's ability to increase the effectiveness of its peace operations

[927] Furthermore, capacities that strengthen personnel safety and the protection of civilians, such as intelligence and transport aircraft contributions, will be emphasized

[928] By participating with requested capacities, Norway can influence reform of UN peacekeeping operations in a credible manner

[929] EU The EU is a key partner for Norway also in security and defense policy

[930] The EU's work on a Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP) is constantly evolving

[931] Security and defense policy issues are increasingly being placed on the agenda of the European Council, where the EU's heads of state and government meet

[932] Norway and the EU have largely overlapping security policy interests and challenges

[933] It is in Norway's interest to help support Europe's crisis management capabilities

[934] Norway has strengthened and will further develop the security policy dialogue with the EU

[935] Close cooperation between NATO and the EU is becoming increasingly important in the face of complex security developments

[936] From the Norwegian side, it is desirable to have the closest possible cooperation with the EU within the framework of the CSDP

[937] Through the administrative agreement from 2006, Norway, as a non-member, is an active participant in the European Defence Agency

[938] European Defence Agency, EDA) work to develop and strengthen European defence capabilities and industrial cooperation

[939] Norway has participated in a number of EU civilian and military crisis management operations and has contributed three times to the Nordic Battlegroup, which is part of the EU's task forces

[940] Norway still has an ambition to participate in CSDP operations where appropriate and relevant

[941] Participation in EU operations and capability development is important in itself, but also strengthens cooperation in general

[942] Nordic countries

[943] Nordic defense cooperation has long traditions, and there is good security policy dialogue between the Nordic countries in several forums

[944] Common belonging to the Euro-Atlantic security community provides the potential for practical and flexible defense cooperation at all levels

[945] Nordic Defence Cooperation (NORDEFCO) is a good framework for security and defence policy dialogue, coordination of efforts in international operations, cooperation on training and exercises in the region, and capability development cooperation

[946] Cooperation has been strengthened in recent years, and security policy developments in our immediate vicinity have further reinforced this development

[947] Over many years, Sweden and Finland have developed an active and close partnership with NATO, where participation in NATO operations in Afghanistan and the Balkans in particular has improved the countries' ability to operate effectively together with Norwegian and allied forces

[948] The recognition of Sweden and Finland's status as Enhanced Opportunities Partners and the signing of host country support agreements at the NATO Summit in Wales in 2014 are important steps in the development of Sweden's and Finland's cooperation with the alliance

[949] The increased Russian military activity, particularly in the Baltic Sea, but also in the High North, underlines the need for a close security policy dialogue between the Nordic countries, within a Nordic-Baltic framework and within NATO and the EU

[950] The Nordic countries have good experience of operating together in international operations and within defense-oriented security sector reform, where the ambition is to further joint contributions to efforts for international peace and security

[951] The UN operation MINUSMA in Mali has strengthened Nordic cooperation on international operations

[952] Among other things, Norway has taken the initiative for a Nordic rotation scheme for transport aircraft in MINUSMA, which can form a model for strengthening the joint peacekeeping effort

[953] Norway plays a central role in NATO's support package to Georgia through coordination of the Nordic-Baltic support package to Georgia's Joint Training and Evaluation Centre (JTEC

[954] Unconventional threats and other developments

[955] The framework conditions for Norwegian security and defense policy are also worsened by cross-border and unconventional threats from terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and threats in digital space

[956] At the same time, a number of other non-military trends also influence the assumptions underlying defense planning

[957] This applies in particular to developments in technology, the use of space, demography and climate

[958] The Government has also in Report

[959] St. 37 (2014–2015) Global security challenges in foreign policy

[960] Terrorism, organized crime, piracy and security challenges in the digital space presented how certain cross-border challenges can be met with foreign and development policy instruments

[961] Terrorism and violent extremism remain a serious threat to national and international peace and security

[962] A number of terrorist attacks and uncovered terrorist plots in recent years show how boundless and complex the threat is

[963] In Norway, terrorist attacks are initially considered serious crimes, but they can take forms that result in them being considered armed attacks in accordance with the UN Charter

[964] The extensive terrorist attacks of recent years also show that handling them is extremely demanding and can challenge liberal societies

[965] Weak government control in several states means that terrorist organizations can establish themselves and operate relatively unhindered in certain areas

[966] Terrorism in combination with organized crime poses a further challenge to weak states and regional stability

[967] Terrorist groups such as ISIL and al-Qaeda have succeeded in conquering extensive areas of land in, among other places, Iraq, Syria, Libya and Yemen

[968] Their behavior has caused great humanitarian suffering and represents a threat to both regional and international security

[969] The land areas they control can be used for planning and facilitating terrorist attacks against countries in their own region as well as against Western countries and also help motivate other groups

[970] The terrorist threat against Norwegian citizens, businesses and interests abroad has increased

[971] Foreign fighters joining terrorist groups to receive military training or participate in combat operations are a serious problem

[972] The terrorist threat also increases in European countries if military knowledge and experience are spread and contribute to radicalization

[973] Foreign fighters from countries in North Africa and the Middle East also pose a risk of spreading extremism when returning to their home countries in the region or by migrating to other countries

[974] Weapons of mass destruction and means of delivery

[975] The proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery is a serious threat to international security

[976] The spread of nuclear weapons expertise to unstable states is in a unique position with its potential for harm, and such weapons going astray could lead to regional destabilization and possible arms races

[977] This could worsen conditions in regions already characterized by conflict and tension, and the risk increases that future conflicts in South or East Asia could take on a nuclear dimension

[978] Chemical and biological weapons and the proliferation of technology related to long-range delivery means could threaten European security and trigger international reactions

[979] Security Council Resolution 1540 gives states binding obligations to adopt national legislation that prevents the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction

[980] Modern cruise missiles and precision-guided ballistic missiles will pose a serious and growing risk to NATO and transatlantic security in the future

[981] NATO's development of territorial missile defense in Europe is one of the most important measures to strengthen the alliance's security against this development

[982] NATO is building a command and control system where nations' voluntary contributions of ballistic missile defense capabilities can be included in NATO's Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD

[983] Work to identify possible Norwegian contributions to NATO's missile defense continues

[984] Norway has been a driving force in the International Atomic Energy Agency's (IAEA) work on safeguards, where their inspection work in Iran in particular has been of crucial importance for non-proliferation in recent years

[985] Norway contributed significantly to the implementation of the nuclear agreement with Iran

[986] Through the Nuclear Security Summits (NSS), Norway has contributed to countering nuclear terrorism

[987] Digitization and digital threats

[988] Norway is one of the most digitalized countries in the world

[989] The rapid development of information and communication technology (ICT) provides completely new opportunities for the defense sector and society at large

[990] An ever-increasing amount of data can be stored, processed, analyzed and shared in near real time

[991] Elevated platforms, such as manned and unmanned aerial platforms and satellites, will increasingly be used for communication purposes

[992] By combining a number of such systems, it will be possible to improve military communications coverage

[993] ICT that is developed for civilian purposes and adapted for military use will constitute an increasing proportion of military ICT as the differences between military and civilian ICT become smaller

[994] Increased dependence on ICT also increases vulnerability to digital threats and attacks

[995] Digital attacks are one of the fastest growing threats to individuals, businesses and public institutions

[996] The attacks can come from both state and non-state actors

[997] Such attacks can challenge our societal security, but they can also pose a threat to state security if critical societal functions are disrupted

[998] NATO has established that digital attacks can have just as serious consequences as conventional attacks

[999] Attacks in the digital space are therefore covered by the NATO Treaty's Article 5 on collective defence

[1000] NATO has adopted a reinforced policy and action plan for defense against digital attacks

[1001] For the defense sector, the greatest threat in peacetime is related to foreign intelligence activities

[1002] Network-based intelligence operations involve the covert collection of large amounts of data, and are a cost-effective alternative to traditional espionage

[1003] Actors are becoming increasingly competent, goal-oriented and adaptable

[1004] The boundless nature of digital space and the possibility of covert and anonymous presence make it difficult to uncover, prevent and deter threat actors

[1005] Offensive cyber operations can be used for intelligence purposes, but also for sabotage actions that can paralyze critical infrastructure and lead to the collapse of key societal functions such as financial services, power supply and communications

[1006] Serious digital attacks early in a conflict can create uncertainty and make it difficult for authorities to manage the crisis

[1007] A potential adversary could exploit such a situation to carry out more traditional military operations

[1008] The warning time for digital attacks can be very short and the attack can be challenging to detect

[1009] In addition, it can be difficult to determine who is behind an attack

[1010] Digital attacks have increasingly become an integral part of military operations

[1011] Such attacks can disrupt, influence and impede national decision-making processes in security crises and armed conflict

[1012] The ability to resist attacks in and through digital space to ensure one’s own freedom of action will therefore be important elements in a country's defense, even though the use of force through digital space will probably not be able to resolve interstate conflicts alone

[1013] A prerequisite for being able to resist such attacks is to have sufficient capacity and a legal framework to be able to detect and handle digital attacks that originate outside Norway's borders

[1014] Technology

[1015] Technological development creates a number of opportunities and challenges for the Armed Forces

[1016] Available technology influences military strategy and tactics, and effective performance of the Armed Forces' tasks requires ongoing and active exploitation of technological opportunities

[1017] Technological developments mean increasing performance and opening up possible technological advantages

[1018] At the same time, this creates more vulnerabilities, increased dependency and complexity in sensor, command and control systems, weapons systems and platforms

[1019] The effects and vulnerabilities resulting from technological developments apply to all domains in which the Armed Forces operate

[1020] Unlike a few decades ago, where technological development was largely driven by military needs, our time is characterized by a greater dispersion in driving forces and environments for the development of new and leading technologies

[1021] The costs of developing and procuring defense equipment are increasing more than the general price increase in society

[1022] The result over time is a steady reduction in the number of units that, in return, have significantly better properties than the previous generation of equipment

[1023] There is, however, a limit to how low the number of units can be before the capacity loses its operational relevance

[1024] Technological development can also occur in larger leaps where new technologies give rise to completely new solutions to operational needs

[1025] This can have consequences for structure, concepts, organization and competence needs

[1026] The emergence of driverless and autonomous systems is one of the most recent examples of this

[1027] Exploitation of space

[1028] Exploitation of space is of increasing importance for critical societal functions

[1029] Space-based communication, navigation and surveillance contribute to the Armed Forces' operational capability, national sovereignty assertion and exercise of authority, especially in the High North

[1030] The military and other actors operating in these areas are increasingly dependent on space-based services

[1031] For example, satellite communications provide coverage where few other communication solutions can reach

[1032] Increasing dependence on the space domain makes us vulnerable to the loss of these services

[1033] As satellite systems become increasingly important for national and societal security, they may become attractive targets for hostile attacks

[1034] Satellite systems are also vulnerable to unintended events such as space weather and operational errors that can disrupt or cause signals to drop out

[1035] In parallel with the development of advanced satellites and large space projects, technological developments and demand for space services have led to ever lower prices for satellites and to the emergence of small satellites

[1036] While satellites in the 1970s were reserved for the great powers, there are now satellites from over 40 countries – including Norway – in orbit around the Earth, and more and more countries will gain access to space in this way

[1037] The application of space capabilities and technology is also increasingly characterized by multi-purpose solutions where the same satellite can simultaneously serve both civilian and military purposes

[1038] Satellite sensors and data that were previously only available for purely military purposes are now increasingly available not only to civilian authorities but also to commercial actors

[1039] The Norwegian-developed surveillance satellite AISSAT (Automatic Identification System Satellite) is an example of a small satellite that has contributed to increased effectiveness at a low cost for, among others, the Norwegian Armed Forces and the Norwegian Coastal Administration

[1040] Strategic communication

[1041] In recent years, targeted communication has become an increasingly important tool for state and non-state actors' efforts to achieve their goals

[1042] At the same time, the complex security policy situation also means that information as a tool in itself becomes a field of tension

[1043] The defense sector's ability to identify and analyze attempts to influence Norway, as well as the ability to support political and military objectives and decisions with strategic communication, must be strengthened

[1044] This primarily involves targeted organization and prioritization of existing resources

[1045] Among NATO countries, strategic communication is defined as the overall use of communication to influence an actor's attitudes and actions

[1046] NATO is increasingly emphasizing strategic communication as an important part of strategy development, decision-making and operations

[1047] Norway will actively participate in and gain expertise from NATO's work in this area

[1048] Potential security policy challenges may occur in smooth transitions between peace and crisis, and between the national and international

[1049] Potential threats may involve a combined use of military, paramilitary, irregular and civilian means

[1050] This challenges the authorities' ability to make good decisions for political and possibly military handling

[1051] Manipulation and use of various communication tools could be part of an adversary's strategy to create ambiguity and doubt about what is happening, and to influence the population and decision-makers

[1052] This could take place alone or in conjunction with the use of military force and coercive diplomacy

[1053] Strategic communication is also used in peacetime to prepare the ground for potential crises and possible armed conflict

[1054] The purpose may be to influence international target groups in advance of a planned conflict, and reduce the likelihood of international intervention

[1055] This is often characterized by one or more of the actors in the initial phases denying their own actions and motives, and attempting to influence the outside world's perceptions of the other party's actions and motives

[1056] It is therefore crucial that the defense sector has both the expertise and resources to identify and analyze this type of instrument at an early stage

[1057] This is necessary to contribute to rapid and good situational understanding, and to support political and military objectives and decisions

[1058] Strategic communication should have a clearer and more prominent role within preparedness and the Armed Forces' operational activities than is the case today

[1059] The defense sector must also be able to contribute to the Norwegian authorities' strategic communication when necessary

[1060] Truthful and timely communication in words and actions should be the guideline for the defense sector, and is the most effective countermeasure if Norway is exposed to propaganda

[1061] Norway must have the ability to coordinate all measures taken by the defense sector in the information domain, as well as have sufficient handling capacity

[1062] A complicating factor surrounding strategic communication is that it crosses established dividing lines, both internally within the defense sector and cross-sectorally

[1063] Effective organization of strategic communication work can therefore appear as an organizational and fundamental challenge

[1064] Through this work, the defense sector will contribute to promoting Norway's strategic interests and supporting the Norwegian authorities' strategic communication

[1065] In addition to its own internal sectoral organization, the defense sector must also contribute effectively to the government's overall efforts within strategic communication

[1066] Demographics and labor market Demographic changes and changes in the labor market affect how the defense sector recruits, develops and uses expertise

[1067] In today's society, the norm is the dual-career family, where the majority of employees have a partner's career, and the needs of the family at large, to take into account in their own career choices

[1068] This challenges the traditional career paths in the Armed Forces with high rotation and frequent relocations and has an impact on the ability to recruit and retain the expertise the Armed Forces needs

[1069] Family policy is an important issue for the Armed Forces

[1070] At a time when greater efforts are required from the Armed Forces, the pressure on the family is increasing, and the Armed Forces may lose skilled employees in whom much has been invested

[1071] Family policy involves, among other things, facilitating flexible and diverse career opportunities, predictability and flexibility in terms of working hours

[1072] Burden distribution during periods of high stress, such as deployment or exercise activity, is also important

[1073] The family perspective must be part of the defense sector's competence policy, strategic competence management and career planning

[1074] This will involve knowledge-based thinking, innovation and highlighting what is already good practice in the area

[1075] Environment and climate

[1076] Environmental and climate change is a disturbing, global challenge

[1077] Global warming can have serious consequences such as rising sea levels, flooding, deforestation and desertification

[1078] This development could affect defense planning and military operations

[1079] Climate change has consequences for the Armed Forces' infrastructure, and may affect the requirements for the Armed Forces' materiel and operations

[1080] Climate change is expected to have the greatest impact, and lead to changes in human activity, in areas of the world where the environment is most vulnerable

[1081] This includes the highlands, where the Armed Forces must be prepared to operate on a larger scale and with the operational and logistical challenges this entails

[1082] Societal developments influence the further development and organization of the Armed Forces

[1083] To reduce the environmental consequences of the Armed Forces' activities, environmental aspects must be an integrated part of defense planning, including in the procurement of materiel, buildings and facilities

[1084] The defense sector must seek to reduce the negative environmental consequences of its own activities, and it is important that existing and new infrastructure is adapted to changing climate conditions with regard to wind, precipitation, rising sea levels, landslides and avalanches

[1085] Environmental protection work in the defense sector includes both prevention of pollution and cleanup of past pollution

[1086] The defense sector must take social responsibility in managing society's assets

[1087] The defense sector's businesses must be drivers in demanding goods and services that satisfy environmental and climate requirements, and must contribute to a green shift within their areas

[1088] The Armed Forces' environmental challenges are particularly related to the use of equipment, which when used in training and exercises can cause adverse environmental impacts, including emissions in the form of noise

[1089] The military is a legitimate user of land for training purposes, and pressures cannot be completely avoided

[1090] The goal must be to minimize the burden through environmentally conscious planning and implementation of activities

[1091] The defense sector's environmental responsibility requires holistic thinking in which measures and instruments are put into context and adapted to specific environmental challenges

[1092] The defense sector must maintain expertise in environmental issues and ensure that knowledge is safeguarded and that new requirements and measures are taken into account in planning for materiel, property, buildings and facilities, exercises, training and operations

[1093] Greenhouse gas emissions from the Armed Forces' equipment vary with activity, including exercise activities and participation in international operations

[1094] The largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in the sector are vessels and aircraft, each of which accounts for more than a third of the sector's total emissions

[1095] Since 2006, the defense sector has, through targeted measures, reduced its consumption of fossil oil for heating by more than 70 percent

[1096] The government's goal to phase out the use of fossil fuel oil as a base load in government buildings by the end of 2018 entails extensive measures in the sector

[1097] The government plans to phase out fossil fuel oil for base load in the Armed Forces' buildings in 2018, in line with the climate agreement

[1098] The defense economy in a long-term perspective Maintaining a defense that can handle changing challenges in the current threat landscape requires a sustained willingness and ability to invest in the Defense through adequate, stable and predictable frameworks, in addition to constant renewal and efficiency improvements within the sector

[1099] The defense sector is in a challenging financial situation at the start of this long-term plan

[1100] The government places crucial emphasis on a holistic approach, including through a significant strengthening of the defense sector's overall funding level, and much-needed modernization and reform

[1101] Report S (2011–2012) did not sufficiently substantiate long-term economic sustainability, particularly because it did not take sufficient account of the cost developments associated with maintaining defense capabilities

[1102] Furthermore, security policy developments have highlighted the need for higher preparedness through increased availability and endurance, and are reinforcing already identified financial challenges in the defense sector

[1103] To ensure financial sustainability in the development of the defense sector, there must be consistency between tasks, structure and finances

[1104] In this long-term plan, the government promotes comprehensive solutions and sets cross-priorities within the entire defense sector

[1105] Like other sectors, the defense sector must make the most of the resources that society makes available

[1106] To create balance, within a defined economic planning framework, the government will prioritize between different capacities

[1107] Individually, all of these appear relevant, but they must still be assessed holistically in the range between what is operationally relevant, security policywise and economically sustainable

[1108] The defense economy is influenced by a number of external factors – primarily by developments in the Norwegian economy and national priorities in fiscal policy

[1109] This is in addition to macroeconomic trends and developments in the international defense economy, especially among our allies

[1110] This long-term plan establishes a good foundation for sustainability in the defense economy, with a better balance between tasks, structure and finances in a long-term perspective

[1111] The chapter briefly explains the defense economic challenges, trends in the defense economy of NATO countries, and points to some prerequisites for further planning work

[1112] Finally, the long-term economic consequences of the government's recommended structure are explained

[1113] The economic challenge picture

[1114] A continuation of the current level of funding to the defense sector will not provide the necessary financial room for maneuver to renew the structure or make the necessary adjustments to the level of activity

[1115] The consequences of such a continued level will include that investments cannot be followed up with the necessary funds for operation and maintenance

[1116] The reasons why the current defense structure cannot be continued, even if the budget level is maintained, are multiple and complex

[1117] In the following, some key factors are highlighted

[1118] The defense sector's share of value creation in Norway

[1119] Previous long-term plans have been largely based on the assumption of stability and low voltage in our local areas

[1120] This has resulted in ongoing operations being prioritized over preparedness, availability and response time

[1121] Since the end of the Cold War, the defense sector's share of the state budget has also been halved

[1122] During the same period, defense spending as a share of GDP has fallen from over 3 percent in 1990 to around 1.5 percent

[1123] At the same time, there has been strong economic growth in Norway

[1124] GDP growth during this period has been over 80 percent

[1125] Low levels of threat and tension in Europe have contributed to other societal tasks being prioritized over defense

[1126] Backlogs due to previous priorities

[1127] The transformation of the Armed Forces into a response force was necessary and correct, and has resulted in Norway having a modern, high-quality defense force

[1128] The Armed Forces have made a formidable and recognized contribution to international operations over time

[1129] The effort has been competency-building and professionalizing for the defense sector's personnel and organization

[1130] The prioritization of ongoing operations has also reduced attention to the Armed Forces' ability to solve the most important and demanding tasks related to the collective defense of Norway and its allies

[1131] The Armed Forces' preparedness and readiness have not been given sufficient priority

[1132] The Government will therefore prioritize increased availability and sustainability of the Armed Forces' capabilities

[1133] Overall, the cost of re-establishing availability and endurance amounts to just under NOK 2.5 billion, and is mainly related to maintenance, emergency logistics and spare parts

[1134] The government has prioritized maintenance and emergency preparedness in the annual budgets, and this work must continue in the coming years to provide a basis for further investment

[1135] Changed security policy situation The framework conditions for Norwegian security have changed, as described in chapters 1 and

[1136] In the future, Norway must be prepared for a new normal situation with increased tension, where challenges to Norwegian or allied security may arise at short notice

[1137] Security policy developments place new demands on the defense sector, and intensify the challenges that can be associated with a lack of responsiveness, availability, and endurance

[1138] The changes not only present operational challenges, but will also be very costly

[1139] Military modernization and development must take place continuously and with a long-term perspective

[1140] Decisions made today have consequences for the defense Norway will have far into the future

[1141] Investments in expensive weapons systems strengthen defense capabilities, while also tying up funds for operation and maintenance

[1142] The breadth of the Armed Forces' capabilities and presence

[1143] The Armed Forces' activities were previously spread over large parts of the country and there has been a great breadth in the Armed Forces' capabilities

[1144] Local bases and facilities have given the Armed Forces visibility in society

[1145] The armed forces will continue to be present throughout the country

[1146] However, it is not sustainable to maintain all established structures, bases and capacities

[1147] Some of these have become less relevant as a result of technological developments and the introduction of new concepts for logistics and support

[1148] A credible defense must be constantly evolving and continuously adapted to requirements and needs

[1149] New needs mean that capacities and bases that no longer have the same priority must be phased out

[1150] The Government will prioritize those capabilities that collectively provide the best defense capability, even if this entails consequences for localization and changes to the structure of the Armed Forces

[1151] Cost developments in the defense sector

[1152] The structure and capabilities of the armed forces must be constantly modernized in accordance with changing threats and challenges, and in order to be able to operate together with allies

[1153] New weapons systems will usually have different characteristics and better performance compared to the equipment they replace

[1154] In this way, the Armed Forces' operational capability is further developed, and the relative balance of power is sought to be maintained

[1155] The need for constant efficiency improvements is also becoming a significant cost-driving factor

[1156] The defense sector is experiencing rapid growth in costs resulting from the need for high-tech and highly advanced equipment, both as a result of changes between generations of major systems, such as fighter aircraft and submarines, and due to upgrade needs within the service life of the material systems

[1157] To date, this cost increase has not been sufficiently taken into account in defense planning, but this is crucial for the defense capability to be maintained over time

[1158] Previous long-term plans have largely used reductions in numbers (volume) and streamlining of operations as means to cover the discrepancy between the expected and actual costs for different capacities

[1159] Operational effectiveness on individual systems has been prioritized over volume and endurance

[1160] In connection with major equipment acquisitions, such as F-16s, frigates and now F-35 fighter jets, partial additional funding has been proposed

[1161] Realizing efficiency gains has been very important for financing the last two long-term plans

[1162] The government will continue and strengthen efficiency work, but it is still not realistic to plan that efficiency alone will be able to cover the cost level that results from constant renewal and modernization

[1163] In this long-term plan, the government bases comprehensive calculations on future cost developments on the capacities included in the proposed structure

[1164] Many of the main systems in the Armed Forces have already been reduced to a number that the Chief of Defence describes as a critical minimum

[1165] It is no longer realistic to further reduce the number of units in the structure without removing entire main systems

[1166] In many cases, this would mean that the cost of maintaining and operating each unit would be disproportionately high compared to the operational value

[1167] Developments in NATO countries' defense economies The financial crisis that began in 2008 had major consequences for the development of defense budgets in most NATO countries

[1168] Member states' defense budgets have stagnated, and in many cases fallen

[1169] of 28 NATO member states reduced their defense budgets from

[1170] The decision from the NATO summit in 2014 to halt the decline in defense budgets, increase defense budgets' share of gross domestic product, and maintain a sufficiently high level of investment has contributed to greater attention being paid to the resource situation in the alliance

[1171] Budget developments showed positive signs

[1172] Allies are expected to have halted the decline in their defence budgets in 2015 and 16 Allies were expected to increase their defence budgets in 2015 in constant prices, while 23 Allies spent more of their defence budget on materiel investments in

[1173] Five member states were expected to meet NATO's two percent target in 2015, compared to three the previous year

[1174] In 2015, eight member states, including Norway, were expected to meet NATO's goal of spending a minimum of 20 percent of the defense budget on materiel investments

[1175] For Norway, it is about taking responsibility and being a predictable and credible ally that invests in modern capabilities, such as fighter aircraft, which also benefits the alliance

[1176] NATO's strategic concept states that the alliance must have sufficient resources in the form of funding, personnel, expertise and military capabilities to carry out its tasks

[1177] Although the jointly financed budgets in NATO are relatively modest compared to the nations' total spending in this area, they are of crucial importance for NATO's joint capabilities, integrated command structure and for the cohesion of the alliance

[1178] The negative budget development in some member states must be reversed to avoid further erosion of the alliance's joint budgets

[1179] A better balance between tasks and resources must be sought

[1180] Increased use of joint funding and joint solutions will help strengthen capability development in NATO

[1181] Norway participates in the alliance's two major joint projects within air surveillance

[1182] Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) and Alliance Ground Surveillance (AGS

[1183] A number of improvement measures have been identified and will be implemented in the coming years to make better use of shared resources

[1184] There is growing concern that the Alliance's current operational framework will not be sustainable when approved joint capabilities are to be put into use in the near future, while political ambitions and new initiatives from the summits are to be realized

[1185] NATO's command structure will come under even greater resource pressure in the years ahead

[1186] Improving the processes related to planning and utilization of shared resources is high on the alliance's agenda

[1187] The Government is actively working to ensure NATO's relevance and credibility in the future

[1188] This requires the alliance to continuously and clearly prioritize between existing tasks and new initiatives

[1189] The resource framework must reflect the current level of ambition and new measures

[1190] Norway helps to support efficiency and reform measures that do not weaken capabilities

[1191] In addition, efforts are being made to ensure that NATO is given sufficient resources to meet new security challenges

[1192] A significant economic boost for the defense sector

[1193] This long-term plan establishes a solid foundation for long-term sustainability in the defense economy

[1194] A better balance between tasks, structure and finances is planned in a long-term perspective, and real, expected cost developments are included in the calculations

[1195] The government is taking a significant economic boost as a basis

[1196] This requires follow-up on the decisions that have already been made regarding financing the fighter aircraft purchase, a gradual strengthening of the defense budget starting in 2017, in addition to extensive efficiency efforts and reductions in the base and support structure

[1197] In the long-term plan, the government proposes that the defense framework will gradually be increased during the planning period to a level in 2020 that is approximately NOK 7.2 billion above the budget path that was the basis at the beginning of the long-term plan for 2017–2020, and which has been the reference in the planning work until the completion of the plan

[1198] This corresponds to approximately NOK 4.1 billion above the balanced budget

[1199] Over the next 20 years, this long-term plan aims to cover a total additional need of approximately 165 billion kroner (2016), which will constitute a lasting and significant investment in the defense sector

[1200] This investment comes in addition to the already planned additional funding for fighter aircraft

[1201] Strict requirements are placed on these resources to be managed efficiently and in line with the choices and priorities made in this long-term plan

[1202] The plan also assumes that all measures within the base and support activities and personnel area are implemented, and that all savings and efficiency potential is realized

[1203] The government's long-term plan means that through savings, changed personnel structure and efficiency improvements, just under NOK 2.5 billion will be released by the end of 2020, and about NOK 40 billion over a period of 20 years

[1204] Costs incurred in the implementation of releasing these funds must be deducted, and are estimated to total approximately NOK 2 billion

[1205] These are mainly personnel-related restructuring costs, which include costs for necessary downsizing
